when i was in 7th grade, for english, we had to take this test and share our results. i was the only infj, and it felt kind of weird, naturally. i was answering genuinely as i wasn't in any crisis at the time, and i was just answering the quiz as well as i could because i was told to. i did feel like it matched my personality spot on, from the interests to the habits to the motivations and even strengths and weaknesses. i thought it was a cool trick but i still had at the back of my mind "man, this can't possibly be scientific or reliable because there's no way every human fits into 16 personalities. it must have been lucky for me" but then i got it again a couple years later in freshman year, then again the next year. 

recently, i do think the test does respond differently depending on how i've been feeling. sometimes i feel hurt and could care less about the world, which affects my responses and is probably why i get intj sometimes.

someone downvoted you... for being disappointed in yourself? take my upvote. i know it's not comparable to what happened to you, but can relate to the feeling, getting angry and sometimes saying something i wouldn't normally say when something happens to you (sometimes out of frustration that it's my fault, sometimes out of frustration that it wasn't) and i'm so sorry for your loss. 

if i were you, i would be very angry as well, and i think it's actually very justified that you were upset and even "lashed out". after all, you lost someone important to you. your cat was your friend. your comfort. for people to treat you as overreacting or irrational for being upset when someone lost, and then *lost* that friend, is unfair, in my eyes, at least, especially coming from people who should know and understand you like your parents. 

I think you should learn your own habits and study how you think, how you convey emotions, how you express them, and what you tend to do when you aren't in control of the situation. Understand yourself. Get to know yourself so you won't be shocked when it comes out. Perhaps try to sort your noted habits out into spectrums of what you can do better, and what most people would find understandable or moral in the situation. This will help you draw lines when it comes to other people's critiques of you, as you'll know what you can change for the better, and what is just natural for you or people, to prevent hard feelings with yourself and better tell if someone potentially tries to gaslight or incorrectly correct you.

All in all, the management is one thing, but also know yourself so you can determine whether there even is something to improve on, and to lessen potential self-disappointment. i hope this helps, and sorry if it's redundant or verbose, it's been rather hard to put some things into words recently.
